TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The paper addresses the "cold start problem" in vision active learning (Page 1)
- Active learning fails to outperform random selection at the first choice due to a biased and outlier initial query (Page 1)
- The proposed solution leverages three advantages of contrastive learning: no annotation requirement, label diversity through pseudo-labels, and typical data identification via contrastive features (Page 1)
- Experiments are conducted on CIFAR-10-LT and three medical imaging datasets: Colon Pathology, Abdominal CT, and Blood Cell Microscope (Page 1)
- The initial query method significantly outperforms existing active querying strategies and surpasses random selection by a large margin (Page 1)
- The solution is foreseen as a simple yet strong baseline for choosing the initial query (Page 1)
- Random selection is considered a baseline because it is independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) to the entire data distribution (Page 2)
- Active querying compromises accuracy and diversity compared to random sampling at the beginning of active learning (Page 2)
- The cold start problem is attributed to two aspects: (i) Biased query and (ii) Outlier query (Page 2)
- Most existing active querying strategies (e.g., BALD, Consistency) are outperformed by random selection in selecting initial queries (Page 2)
- Some classes are not selected by active querying strategies due to selection bias (Page 2)
- The cold start problem is addressed in vision active learning for the first time (Page 3)
- Two explicit criteria for annotation importance are label diversity and inclusion of typical data (Page 3)
- The proposed method uses K-means clustering with pseudo-labels to enforce label diversity (Page 3)
- The number of clusters (K) is set to 30 in experiments, given 9, 11, and 8 ground-truth classes (Page 3)
- Contrastive methods like MoCo, SimCLR, and BYOL are suggested for generating features for clustering (Page 3)
- The solution can be used as a strong baseline for initial query selection in image classification (Page 3)

SECTION: 3 Experimental Results (Pages 5-8)

TOPICS: active querying, dataset maps, self-supervised contrastive learning, label diversity, cold start problem, long-tail distributions, AUC scores, class coverage, querying strategies, benchmarking

TEXT_EVIDENCE:
- The paper defines "hard-to-contrast" data as those with low confidence values in the instance discrimination task (Page 5)
- Confidence ($\hat{\mu}_m$) is calculated across $E$ epochs using Equation 3 (Page 5)
- The proposed active querying strategy includes three steps: feature extraction via self-supervised contrastive learning, K-means clustering for label diversity, and selecting hard-to-contrast data (Page 5)
- The method is compared to a baseline that requires manual annotations and suffers from poor label diversity (Page 5)
- Both easy-to-learn and hard-to-contrast data achieve compelling performance, but the latter is more practical (Page 5)
- The experimental section begins by stating that the method will be tested on long-tail datasets to simulate real-world scenarios (Page 5)
- Diversity is a significant add-on to most querying strategies, improving or maintaining performance (Page 6)
- Coreset works very well because it implicitly considers label diversity by formulating a K-center problem (Page 6)
- The proposed querying strategy covers 100% of classes in most low-budget scenarios using low budgets (≤ 0.002% of MedMNIST) (Page 6)
- Some results are missing (marked as “-”) because the querying strategy fails to sample at least one data point for each class (Page 6)
- Baselines include random selection, Max-Entropy, Margin, Consistency, BALD, VAAL, and Coreset (Page 6)
- For contrastive learning, MoCo v2 was trained for 200 epochs with default hyperparameters (Page 6)
- UMAP is used to analyze feature clustering results (Page 6)
- Hard-to-contrast querying strategy significantly outperforms random selection by 1.8%, 2.6%, and 5.2% on PathMNIST, OrganAMNIST, and BloodMNIST respectively when querying 0.1% of the dataset (Page 7)
- On CIFAR-10-LT, hard-to-contrast outperforms random selection by 21.2% and 24.1% when querying 20% and 30% of the dataset (Page 7)
- The proposed strategy covers 100% of classes in low budget scenarios (≤0.002% of full dataset) by integrating K-means clustering with contrastive features (Page 7)
- Easy-to-learn and hard-to-learn strategies require ground truths, making them impractical for active learning, whereas hard-to-contrast is label-free (Page 7)
- The paper examines the cold start problem in vision active learning and proposes a solution (Page 8)
- The "hard-to-contrast" data selection criterion is shown to be superior to existing methods (Page 8)
- A strong positive correlation exists between AUC₂₀ (starting) and AUC₅₀ (ending) for all strategies, with values ranging from r = 0.67 to 0.92 (Page 8)
- This correlation remains high when fine-tuning from MoCo v2, with r values from 0.70 to 0.92 (Page 8)
- The initial query is consequential regardless of model initialization, and the cold start problem persists even with pre-trained models (Page 8)
- The study provides an empirical benchmark, leaving theoretical analyses for future work (Page 8)

Our initial query not only significantly outperforms existing active querying strategies but also surpasses random selection by a large margin. elements.text: Making Your First Choice: To Address Cold Start Problem in Vision Active Learning

Liangyu Chen<sup>1</sup> Yutong Bai<sup>2</sup> Siyu Huang<sup>3</sup> Yongyi Lu<sup>2</sup>  
Bihan Wen<sup>1</sup> Alan L. Yuille<sup>2</sup> Zongwei Zhou<sup>2,*</sup>
$^{1}$ Nanyang Technological University  $^{2}$ Johns Hopkins University  $^{3}$ Harvard University
Abstract

Active learning promises to improve annotation efficiency by iteratively selecting the most important data to be annotated first. However, we uncover a striking contradiction to this promise: active learning fails to select data as efficiently as random selection at the first few choices. We identify this as the cold start problem in vision active learning, caused by a biased and outlier initial query. This paper seeks to address the cold start problem by exploiting the three advantages of contrastive learning: (1) no annotation is required; (2) label diversity is ensured by pseudo-labels to mitigate bias; (3) typical data is determined by contrastive features to reduce outliers. Experiments are conducted on CIFAR-10-LT and three medical imaging datasets (i.e. Colon Pathology, Abdominal CT, and Blood Cell Microscope). Our initial query not only significantly outperforms existing active querying strategies but also surpasses random selection by a large margin. We foresee our solution to the cold start problem as a simple yet strong baseline to choose the initial query for vision active learning.
Code is available: https://github.com/c-liangyu/CSVAL
1 Introduction
"The secret of getting ahead is getting started."
— Mark Twain

The cold start problem was initially found in recommender systems [56, 39, 9, 23] when algorithms had not gathered sufficient information about users with no purchase history. It also occurred in many other fields, such as natural language processing [55, 33] and computer vision [5, 11, 38] during the active learning procedure<sup>1</sup>. Active learning promises to improve annotation efficiency by iteratively selecting the most important data to annotate. However, we uncover a striking contradiction to this promise: Active learning fails to select data as effectively as random selection at the first choice. We identify this as the cold start problem in vision active learning and illustrate the problem using three medical imaging applications (Figure 1a-c) as well as a natural imaging application (Figure 1d). Cold start is a crucial topic [54, 30] because a performant initial query can lead to noticeably improved subsequent cycle performance in the active learning procedure, evidenced in §3.3. There is a lack of studies that systematically illustrate the cold start problem, investigate its causes, and provide practical solutions to address it. To this end, we ask: What causes the cold start problem and how can we select the initial query when there is no labeled data available?
*Corresponding author: Zongwei Zhou (zzhou82@jh.edu)

Active learning aims to select the most important data from the unlabeled dataset and query human experts to annotate new data. The newly annotated data is then added to improve the model. This process can be repeated until the model reaches a satisfactory performance level or the annotation budget is exhausted.
Preprint. Under review.

1 Introduction
"The secret of getting ahead is getting started."
— Mark Twain

The cold start problem was initially found in recommender systems [56, 39, 9, 23] when algorithms had not gathered sufficient information about users with no purchase history. It also occurred in many other fields, such as natural language processing [55, 33] and computer vision [5, 11, 38] during the active learning procedure<sup>1</sup>. Active learning promises to improve annotation efficiency by iteratively selecting the most important data to annotate. However, we uncover a striking contradiction to this promise: Active learning fails to select data as effectively as random selection at the first choice. We identify this as the cold start problem in vision active learning and illustrate the problem using three medical imaging applications (Figure 1a-c) as well as a natural imaging application (Figure 1d). Cold start is a crucial topic [54, 30] because a performant initial query can lead to noticeably improved subsequent cycle performance in the active learning procedure, evidenced in §3.3. There is a lack of studies that systematically illustrate the cold start problem, investigate its causes, and provide practical solutions to address it. To this end, we ask: What causes the cold start problem and how can we select the initial query when there is no labeled data available?
*Corresponding author: Zongwei Zhou (zzhou82@jh.edu)

Active learning aims to select the most important data from the unlabeled dataset and query human experts to annotate new data. The newly annotated data is then added to improve the model. This process can be repeated until the model reaches a satisfactory performance level or the annotation budget is exhausted.
Preprint. Under review.

pages.summary:
This page introduces a study on the "cold start problem" in vision active learning, particularly in medical image analysis. It identifies two key criteria for effective initial query selection: label diversity and inclusion of typical data. The authors propose a method using K-means clustering with pseudo-labels to ensure label diversity and contrastive learning features to identify typical data, addressing the cold start issue. The paper reviews related work from recommender systems and NLP, and outlines its contributions and methodology in Section 2.

**Text Evidence:**
- The cold start problem is addressed in vision active learning for the first time.
- Two explicit criteria for annotation importance are label diversity and inclusion of typical data.
- The proposed method uses K-means clustering with pseudo-labels to enforce label diversity.
- The number of clusters (K) is set to 30 in experiments, given 9, 11, and 8 ground-truth classes.
- Contrastive methods like MoCo, SimCLR, and BYOL are suggested for generating features for clustering.
- The solution can be used as a strong baseline for initial query selection in image classification.

We consider the data with a low confidence value (Equation 3) as "hard-to-contrast" because they are seldom predicted correctly in the instance discrimination task. Apparently, if the model cannot distinguish a data point with others, this data point is expected to carry typical characteristics that are shared across the dataset [40]. Visually, hard-to-contrast data gather in the bottom region of the Dataset Maps and "easy-to-contrast" data gather in the top region. As expected, hard-to-learn data are more typical, possessing the most common visual patterns as the entire dataset; whereas easy-to-learn data appear like outliers [54, 26], which may not follow the majority data distribution (examples in Figure 3a and Figure 3c). Additionally, we also plot the original Dataset Map [12, 48] in Figure 3b, which grouped data into hard-to-learn and easy-to-learn<sup>4</sup>. Although the results in §3.2 show equally compelling performance achieved by both easy-to-learn [48] and hard-to-contrast data (ours), the latter do not require any manual annotation, and therefore are more practical and suitable for vision active learning. In summary, to meet the both criteria, our proposed active querying strategy includes three steps: (i) extracting features by self-supervised contrastive learning, (ii) assigning clusters by  $K$ -means algorithm for label diversity, and (iii) selecting hard-to-contrast data from dataset maps. 3 Experimental Results Datasets & metrics. This page presents a method for active querying in vision tasks using Dataset Maps, comparing two strategies: one based on ground truth labels and another based on pseudo-labels. The text explains that "hard-to-contrast" data, identified by low confidence values from self-supervised contrastive learning, are more typical of the dataset and are preferable for training as they alleviate the cold start problem. Figure 3 visually demonstrates this concept with three panels: (a) an overall distribution of data points, (b) a map stratified by ground truth labels showing easy-to-learn and hard-to-learn data, and (c) a map using pseudo-labels to identify easy-to-contrast and hard-to-contrast data. The proposed strategy is label-free and selects data representing common patterns, making it more practical than methods requiring manual annotation.

- The method is compared to a baseline that requires manual annotations and suffers from poor label diversity.
- The results show that both easy-to-learn and hard-to-contrast data achieve compelling performance, but the latter is more practical.

pages.summary:
This page presents a method for active querying in vision tasks using Dataset Maps, comparing two strategies: one based on ground truth labels and another based on pseudo-labels. The text explains that "hard-to-contrast" data, identified by low confidence values from self-supervised contrastive learning, are more typical of the dataset and are preferable for training as they alleviate the cold start problem. Figure 3 visually demonstrates this concept with three panels: (a) an overall distribution of data points, (b) a map stratified by ground truth labels showing easy-to-learn and hard-to-learn data, and (c) a map using pseudo-labels to identify easy-to-contrast and hard-to-contrast data. The proposed strategy is label-free and selects data representing common patterns, making it more practical than methods requiring manual annotation.

Table 1: Diversity is a significant add-on to most querying strategies. AUC scores of different querying strategies are compared on three medical imaging datasets. In either low budget (i.e.  $0.5\%$  or  $1\%$  of MedMNIST datasets) or high budget (i.e.  $10\%$  or  $20\%$  of CIFAR-10-LT) regimes, both random and active querying strategies benefit from enforcing the label diversity of the selected data. The cells are highlighted in blue when adding diversity performs no worse than the original querying strategies. Coreset [41] works very well as its original form because this querying strategy has implicitly considered the label diversity (also verified in Table 2) by formulating a  $K$ -center problem, which selects  $K$  data points to represent the entire dataset. Some results are missing (marked as “-”) because the querying strategy fails to sample at least one data point for each class. Results of more sampling ratios are presented in Appendix Figures 6, 9. Table 2: Class coverage of selected data. Compared with random selection (i.i.d. to entire data distribution), most active querying strategies contain selection bias to specific classes, so the class coverage in their selections might be poor, particularly using low budgets. As seen, using  $0.002\%$  or even smaller proportion of MedMNIST datasets, the class coverage of active querying strategies is much lower than random selection. By integrating  $K$ -means clustering with contrastive features, our querying strategy is capable of covering  $100\%$  classes in most scenarios using low budgets ( $\leq 0.002\%$  of MedMNIST). We also found that our querying strategy covers the most of the classes in the CIFAR-10-LT dataset, which is designatedly more imbalanced. in MedMNIST [53] are used: PathMNIST (colorectal cancer tissue histopathological images), BloodMNIST (microscopic peripheral blood cell images), OrganAMNIST (axial view abdominal CT images of multiple organs). OrganAMNIST is augmented following Azizi et al. [3], while the others following Chen et al. [15]. Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) and Accuracy are used as the evaluation metrics. All results were based on at least three independent runs, and particularly, 100 independent runs for random selection. UMAP [35] is used to analyze feature clustering results. Baselines & implementations. We benchmark a total of seven querying strategies: (1) random selection, (2) Max-Entropy [52], (3) Margin [4], (4) Consistency [18], (5) BALD [28], (6) VAAL [45], and (7) Coreset [41]. For contrastive learning, we trained 200 epochs with MoCo v2, following its default hyperparameter settings. We set  $\tau$  to 0.05 in equation 2. Compared with random selection (i.i.d. to entire data distribution), most active querying strategies contain selection bias to specific classes, so the class coverage in their selections might be poor, particularly using low budgets. As seen, using  $0.002\%$  or even smaller proportion of MedMNIST datasets, the class coverage of active querying strategies is much lower than random selection. By integrating  $K$ -means clustering with contrastive features, our querying strategy is capable of covering  $100\%$  classes in most scenarios using low budgets ( $\leq 0.002\%$  of MedMNIST). 3.1 Contrastive Features Enable Label Diversity to Mitigate Bias Label coverage & diversity. Most active querying strategies have selection bias towards specific classes, thus the class coverage in their selections might be poor (see Table 2), particularly at low budgets. By simply enforcing label diversity to these querying strategies can significantly improve the performance (see Table 1), which suggests that the label diversity is one of the causes that existing active querying strategies perform poorer than random selection. Our proposed active querying strategy, however, is capable of covering  $100\%$  classes in most low budget scenarios ( $\leq 0.002\%$  of full dataset) by integrating  $K$ -means clustering with contrastive features. 3.2 Pseudo-labels Query Hard-to-Contrast Data and Avoid Outliers Hard-to-contrast data are practical for cold start problem. Figure 4 presents the quantitative comparison of four map-based querying strategies, wherein easy- or hard-to-learn are selected by the maps based on ground truths, easy- or hard-to-contrast are selected by the maps based on pseudolabels. Note that easy- or hard-to-learn are enforced with label diversity, due to their class-stratified distributions in the projected 2D space (illustrated in Figure 3). Results suggest that selecting easy-to-learn or hard-to-contrast data contribute to the optimal models. In any case, easy- or hard-to-learn data can not be selected without knowing ground truths, so these querying strategies are not practical for active learning procedure. Selecting hard-to-contrast, on the other hand, is a label-free strategy and yields the highest performance amongst existing active querying strategies (reviewed in Figure 1). More importantly, hard-to-contrast querying strategy significantly outperforms random selection by  $1.8\%$  ( $94.14\% \pm 1.0\%$  vs.  $92.27\% \pm 2.2\%$ ),  $2.6\%$  ( $84.35\% \pm 0.7\%$  vs.  $81.75\% \pm 2.1\%$ ), and  $5.2\%$  ( $88.51\% \pm 1.5\%$  vs.  $83.36\% \pm 3.5\%$ ) on PathMNIST, OrganAMNIST, and BloodMNIST, respectively, by querying  $0.1\%$  of entire dataset. Similarly on CIFAR-10-LT, hard-to-contrast significantly outperforms random selection by  $21.2\%$  ( $87.35\% \pm 0.0\%$  vs.  $66.12\% \pm 0.9\%$ ) and  $24.1\%$  ( $90.59\% \pm 0.1\%$  vs.  $66.53\% \pm 0.5\%$ ) by querying  $20\%$  and  $30\%$  of entire dataset respectively. Note that easy- or hard-to-learn are not enforced with label diversity, for a more informative comparison. 3.3 On the Importance of Selecting Superior Initial Query A good start foresees improved active learning. The Pearson correlation coefficient between  $\mathrm{AUC}_{20}$  (starting) and  $\mathrm{AUC}_{50}$  (ending) shows strong positive correlation ( $r = 0.79$ , 0.80, 0.91, 0.67, 0.92 for random selection, Entropy, Margin, BALD, and Coreset, respectively). Hard-to-contrast data (our proposal) consistently outperforms the others on OrganAMNIST (Figure 5), BloodMNIST (Figure 13), and PathMNIST (Figure 14), and steadily improves the model performances within the next active learning cycles. The initial query is consequential regardless of model initialization. A pre-trained model can improve the performance of each active learning cycle for both random and active selection [55], but the cold start problem remains (evidenced in Figure 14b). This suggests that the model instability and data scarcity are two independent issues to be addressed for the cold start problem. Our "hard-to-contrast" data selection criterion only exploits contrastive learning (an improved model), but also determines the typical data to be annotated first (a better query). As a result, when fine-tuning from MoCo v2, the Pearson correlation coefficient between  $\mathrm{AUC}_{20}$  and  $\mathrm{AUC}_{50}$  remains high ( $r = 0.92$ , 0.81, 0.70, 0.82, 0.85 for random selection, Entropy, Margin, BALD, and Coreset, respectively) and statistically significant ( $p < 0.05$ ). 4 Conclusion This paper systematically examines the causes of the cold start problem in vision active learning and offers a practical and effective solution to address this problem. Analytical results indicate that (1) the level of label diversity and (2) the inclusion of hard-to-contrast data are two explicit criteria to determine the annotation importance. To this end, we devise a novel active querying strategy that can enforce label diversity and determine hard-to-contrast data. The results of three medical imaging and two natural imaging datasets show that our initial query not only significantly outperforms existing active querying strategies but also surpasses random selection by a large margin. This finding is significant because it is the first few choices that define the efficacy and efficiency of the subsequent learning procedure. We foresee our solution to the cold start problem as a simple, yet strong, baseline to sample the initial query for active learning in image classification. Limitation. This study provides an empirical benchmark of initial queries in active learning, while more theoretical analyses can be provided. Yehuda et al. [54] also found that the choice of active learning strategies depends on the initial query budget. A challenge is to articulate the quantity of determining active learning strategies, which we leave for future work.

The Pearson correlation coefficient between  $\mathrm{AUC}_{20}$  (starting) and  $\mathrm{AUC}_{50}$  (ending) shows strong positive correlation ( $r = 0.79$ , 0.80, 0.91, 0.67, 0.92 for random selection, Entropy, Margin, BALD, and Coreset, respectively). This result is statistically significant ( $p < 0.05$ ). Hard-to-contrast data (our proposal) consistently outperforms the others on OrganAMNIST (Figure 5), BloodMNIST (Figure 13), and PathMNIST (Figure 14), and steadily improves the model performances within the next active learning cycles. The initial query is consequential regardless of model initialization. A pre-trained model can improve the performance of each active learning cycle for both random and active selection [55], but the cold start problem remains (evidenced in Figure 14b). This suggests that the model instability and data scarcity are two independent issues to be addressed for the cold start problem. Our "hard-to-contrast" data selection criterion only exploits contrastive learning (an improved model), but also determines the typical data to be annotated first (a better query). As a result, when fine-tuning from MoCo v2, the Pearson correlation coefficient between  $\mathrm{AUC}_{20}$  and  $\mathrm{AUC}_{50}$  remains high ( $r = 0.92$ , 0.81, 0.70, 0.82, 0.85 for random selection, Entropy, Margin, BALD, and Coreset, respectively) and statistically significant ( $p < 0.05$ ). 4 Conclusion This paper systematically examines the causes of the cold start problem in vision active learning and offers a practical and effective solution to address this problem. Analytical results indicate that (1) the level of label diversity and (2) the inclusion of hard-to-contrast data are two explicit criteria to determine the annotation importance. To this end, we devise a novel active querying strategy that can enforce label diversity and determine hard-to-contrast data. The results of three medical imaging and two natural imaging datasets show that our initial query not only significantly outperforms existing active querying strategies but also surpasses random selection by a large margin. This finding is significant because it is the first few choices that define the efficacy and efficiency of the subsequent learning procedure. We foresee our solution to the cold start problem as a simple, yet strong, baseline to sample the initial query for active learning in image classification. Limitation. This study provides an empirical benchmark of initial queries in active learning, while more theoretical analyses can be provided. Yehuda et al. [54] also found that the choice of active learning strategies depends on the initial query budget. A challenge is to articulate the quantity of determining active learning strategies, which we leave for future work.

pages.summary:
This page presents a comprehensive analysis of active learning in vision tasks, focusing on the "cold start problem" and proposing a novel solution based on selecting "hard-to-contrast" data. The main content includes textual discussion of experimental results, a detailed conclusion summarizing the paper's contributions, and Figure 5, which visually compares five different active learning strategies (Random, Entropy, Margin, BALD, Coreset) under two conditions: training from scratch and fine-tuning from self-supervised pre-training. The figure demonstrates that the proposed "hard-to-contrast" method consistently outperforms other initial queries across all cycles on the OrganAMNIST dataset. Key findings include strong positive correlations between initial and final model performance (AUC scores), with specific Pearson correlation coefficients provided for both training scenarios.

**Text Evidence:**
- The paper examines the cold start problem in vision active learning and proposes a solution.
- The "hard-to-contrast" data selection criterion is shown to be superior to existing methods.
- A strong positive correlation exists between AUC₂₀ (starting) and AUC₅₀ (ending) for all strategies, with values ranging from r = 0.67 to 0.92.
- This correlation remains high when fine-tuning from MoCo v2, with r values from 0.70 to 0.92.
- The initial query is consequential regardless of model initialization, and the cold start problem persists even with pre-trained models.
- The study provides an empirical benchmark, leaving theoretical analyses for future work.

4 Conclusion

This paper systematically examines the causes of the cold start problem in vision active learning and offers a practical and effective solution to address this problem. Analytical results indicate that (1) the level of label diversity and (2) the inclusion of hard-to-contrast data are two explicit criteria to determine the annotation importance. To this end, we devise a novel active querying strategy that can enforce label diversity and determine hard-to-contrast data. The results of three medical imaging and two natural imaging datasets show that our initial query not only significantly outperforms existing active querying strategies but also surpasses random selection by a large margin. This finding is significant because it is the first few choices that define the efficacy and efficiency of the subsequent learning procedure. We foresee our solution to the cold start problem as a simple, yet strong, baseline to sample the initial query for active learning in image classification.

Limitation. This study provides an empirical benchmark of initial queries in active learning, while more theoretical analyses can be provided. Yehuda et al. [54] also found that the choice of active learning strategies depends on the initial query budget. A challenge is to articulate the quantity of determining active learning strategies, which we leave for future work.

pages.ocr_text: Potential societal impacts. Real-world data often exhibit long-tailed distributions, rather than the ideal uniform distributions over each class. We improve active learning by enforcing label diversity and hard-to-contrast data. However, we only extensively test our strategies on academic datasets. In many other real-world domains such as robotics and autonomous driving, the data may impose additional constraints on annotation accessibility or learning dynamics, e.g., being fair or private. We focus on standard accuracy and AUC as our evaluation metrics while ignoring other ethical issues in imbalanced data, especially in underrepresented minority classes. pages.ocr_text: Potential societal impacts. Real-world data often exhibit long-tailed distributions, rather than the ideal uniform distributions over each class. We improve active learning by enforcing label diversity and hard-to-contrast data. However, we only extensively test our strategies on academic datasets. In many other real-world domains such as robotics and autonomous driving, the data may impose additional constraints on annotation accessibility or learning dynamics, e.g., being fair or private. We focus on standard accuracy and AUC as our evaluation metrics while ignoring other ethical issues in imbalanced data, especially in underrepresented minority classes. It describes four datasets—PathMNIST, BloodMNIST, OrganAMNIST, and CIFAR-10-LT—with their respective image counts and category numbers, along with their train/validation/test splits. Pre-training Settings. Our settings mostly follow [15, 14]. Table 3a summarizes our contrastive pre-training settings on MedMNIST, following [15]. Table 3a shows the corresponding pre-training settings on CIFAR-10-LT, following the official MoCo demo on CIFAR-10 [14]. The contrastive learning model is pre-trained on 2 NVIDIA RTX3090 GPUs with 24GB memory each. The total number of model parameters is 55.93 million, among which 27.97 million requires gradient backpropagation. Dataset Augmentation. We apply the same augmentation as in MoCo v2 [15] on all the images of RGB modalities to reproduce the optimal augmentation pipeline proposed by the authors, including PathMNIST, BloodMNIST, CIFAR-10-LT. Because OrganAMNIST is a grey scale CT image dataset, we apply the augmentation in [3] designed for radiological images, replacing random gray scale and Gaussian blur with random rotation. Table 4 shows the details of data augmentation. Repeated Augmentation. Our MoCo v2 pre-training is so fast in computation that data loading becomes a new bottleneck that dominates running time in our setup. We perform repeated augmentation on MedMNIST datasets at the level of dataset, also to enlarge augmentation space and improve generalization. [21] proposed repeated augmentation in a growing batch mode to improve generalization and convergence speed by reducing variances. This approach provokes a challenge in computing resources. Recent works [21, 50, 7] proved that fixed batch mode also boosts generalization and optimization by increasing multiplicity of augmentations as well as parameter updates and decreasing the number of unique samples per batch, which holds the batch size fixed. Because the original contrastive learning works [13, 15] were implemented on ImageNet dataset, we attempt to simulate the quantity of ImageNet per epoch to achieve optimal performances. The details are shown in Table 5. We only applied repeated augmentation on MedMNIST, but not CIFAR-10-LT. This is because we follow all the settings of the official CIFAR-10 demo [14] in which repeated augmentation is not employed.

This page details the pre-training settings for contrastive learning models on MedMNIST and CIFAR-10-LT datasets, referencing prior work [15, 14]. It presents two main tables: Table 3a outlines the settings for MedMNIST pre-training, including a ResNet-50 backbone, SGD optimizer, and 200 epochs, while Table 3b shows the settings for CIFAR-10-LT with 800 epochs. The text explains that data augmentation differs between RGB modalities (using MoCo v2's pipeline) and the grayscale OrganAMNIST dataset (using radiological image augmentations). A key focus is on repeated augmentation to overcome data loading bottlenecks, which is applied to MedMNIST but not CIFAR-10-LT to adhere to the official demo's settings.

**Text Evidence:**
- Pre-training uses 2 NVIDIA RTX3090 GPUs with 24GB memory each.
- The model has 55.93 million total parameters, with 27.97 million requiring gradient backpropagation.
- For MedMNIST, pre-training runs for 200 epochs with a batch size of 4096, while CIFAR-10-LT runs for 800 epochs with a batch size of 512.
- Repeated augmentation is used for MedMNIST to improve generalization but is not used for CIFAR-10-LT to follow the official demo [14].
- Data augmentation for RGB images includes hflip, crop, color jitter, gray scale, and Gaussian blur, while OrganAMNIST uses rotation instead of gray scale and Gaussian blur.

This page details the experimental setup for benchmarking active learning methods on MedMNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. It presents two key tables: Table 5, which outlines a "repeated augmentation" technique to accelerate model convergence by increasing the effective number of training samples per epoch, and Table 6, which specifies the standard "benchmark settings" used across all experiments, including the Inception-ResNet-v2 backbone, SGD optimizer, and various data augmentations. The text also references results in other tables and figures (Table 1, 7, Figure 4, Figure 1) and notes that all benchmark experiments were run on NVIDIA RTX 1080 GPUs.

- Benchmark experiments are performed on NVIDIA RTX 1080 GPUs using the settings detailed in Table 6.
- A "cold start" comparison is made between active querying criteria and random selection, referencing Figure 1.
- Repeated augmentation is applied to MedMNIST to reproduce large batch sizes and iteration numbers for faster convergence.

B.2 Contrastive Features Enable Label Diversity to Mitigate Bias Our proposed active querying strategy is capable of covering the majority of classes in most low budget scenarios by integrating K-means clustering and contrastive features, including the tail classes (e.g. femur-left, basophil). Compared to the existing active querying criteria, we achieve the best class coverage of selected query among all budgets presented in Table 2.

Figure: (a) OrganAMNIST

Figure: (b) BloodMNIST; Figure 7: [Continued from Figure 2] Our querying strategy yields better label diversity. Random on the leftmost denotes the class distribution of randomly queried samples, which can also reflect the approximate class distribution of the entire dataset. As seen, even with a relatively larger initial query budget (691 images,  $2\%$  of OrganAMNIST, and 2,391 images,  $20\%$  of BloodMNIST), most active querying strategies are biased towards certain classes. For example in OrganAMNIST, VAAL prefers selecting data in the femur-right and platelet class, but largely ignores data in the lung, liver and monocyte classes. On the contrary, our querying strategy not only selects more data from minority classes (e.g., femur-left and basophil) while retaining the class distribution of major classes.

Selected Query Visualization. To ease the analysis, we project the image features (extracted by a trained MoCo v2 encoder) onto a 2D space by UMAP [35]. The assigned pseudo labels have large overlap with ground truths, suggesting that the features from MoCo v2 are quite discriminative for each class. Overall, Figure 8 shows that hard-to-contrast queries have a greater spread within each cluster than easy-to-contrast ones. Both strategies can cover  $100\%$  classes. Nevertheless, we notice that easy-to-contrast selects local outliers in clusters: samples that do not belong to the majority class in a cluster. Such behavior will invalidate the purpose of clustering, which is to query uniformly by separating classes. Additionally, it possibly exposes the risk of introducing out-of-distribution data to the query, which undermines active learning [26].

Figure: (a) PathMNIST

Figure: (b) OrganAMNIST

Figure: Figure 8: Visualization of  $K$ -means clustering and our active selection. UMAP [35] is used to visualize the feature clustering. Colors indicate the ground truth. Contrastive features clustered by the  $K$ -means algorithm present a fairly clear separation in the 2D space, which helps enforce the label diversity without the need of ground truth. The crosses denote the selected easy- (top) and hard-to-contrast (bottom) data. Overall, hard-to-contrast data have a greater spread within each cluster than easy-to-contrast ones. The figure compares two active learning query selection strategies: "easy-to-contrast" (top row) and "hard-to-contrast" (bottom row). Both methods cover 100% of the classes, but the behavior of the easy-to-contrast strategy is problematic for effective clustering.

elements.text: Selected Query Visualization. To ease the analysis, we project the image features (extracted by a trained MoCo v2 encoder) onto a 2D space by UMAP [35]. The assigned pseudo labels have large overlap with ground truths, suggesting that the features from MoCo v2 are quite discriminative for each class. Overall, Figure 8 shows that hard-to-contrast queries have a greater spread within each cluster than easy-to-contrast ones. Both strategies can cover  $100\%$  classes. Nevertheless, we notice that easy-to-contrast selects local outliers in clusters: samples that do not belong to the majority class in a cluster. Such behavior will invalidate the purpose of clustering, which is to query uniformly by separating classes. Additionally, it possibly exposes the risk of introducing out-of-distribution data to the query, which undermines active learning [26].

This page presents experimental results comparing active learning querying strategies on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-10-LT datasets, focusing on the importance of label diversity. The main finding is that enforcing label diversity significantly improves performance, especially in low-budget scenarios on the highly imbalanced CIFAR-10-LT dataset, where many standard methods fail to sample all classes. The text references Figure 9 (not shown) to illustrate that the proposed strategy achieves a more balanced class distribution compared to other methods.

**Text Evidence:**
- Label diversity is a significant add-on to most querying strategies on the imbalanced CIFAR-10-LT dataset.
- CIFAR-10-LT is more imbalanced than MedMNIST, and the performance gain from label diversity is larger.
- Most active querying strategies fail to query all classes even at larger initial budgets.
- The proposed strategy using K-means clustering and contrastive features covers the majority of classes, including tail classes (horse, ship, truck).
- The proposed method achieves the best class coverage and has the highest proportion of minor classes among all methods.

Our proposed active querying strategy is capable of covering the majority of classes in most low budget scenarios by integrating K-means clustering and contrastive features, including the tail classes (horse, ship, and truck). This page presents Figure 11, which illustrates an active querying strategy based on dataset maps for the PathMNIST and OrganAMNIST datasets. The figure displays the overall distribution of data in (a) and (d), and two types of data maps: one using ground truth labels in (b) and (e), and another using pseudo-labels in (c) and (f). These maps plot data points by confidence and variability, allowing for the selection of "easy-to-learn" and "hard-to-learn" samples from ground truth maps, or "easy-to-contrast" and "hard-to-contrast" samples from pseudo-label maps. The text explains that the ground truth method requires manual annotations and suffers from poor label diversity, while the pseudo-label method is label-free and selects data representing common patterns, which helps alleviate the cold start problem.

**Text Evidence:**
- Figure 11 shows active querying based on Dataset Maps for PathMNIST and OrganAMNIST.
- Ground truth-based querying requires manual annotations and leads to poor label diversity in selected queries.
- Pseudo-label-based querying is label-free and selects "hard-to-contrast" data, which represent the most common patterns in the dataset.
- This strategy alleviates the cold start problem by selecting more suitable data for training.
